opus-5.5.text:
I don't fully agree with that view. In information intelligence, the large companies do have real advantages: data, compute, users, distribution, and capital. Foundation models in particular are very expensive to train, so only a handful of players can compete at that layer. In that sense, yes, the big companies hold a strong position.

But I've seen several technology waves, from PCs to the internet to mobile to cloud, and in every one people said the incumbents had already won. Then a new generation of companies emerged. Each time the underlying platform changes, the way applications are built changes, the business models change, and the user's relationship with technology changes. Incumbents tend to optimize what they already have. They have legacy products, organizational inertia, and revenue they must protect. That creates openings.

I think of it in layers. At the foundation model layer, opportunities for startups are limited. That is a game of scale. Above that, though, in vertical models, agents, tools, and especially applications that deeply understand a specific industry or workflow, the space is enormous. The big companies can't do everything. They can't go deep into every scenario, whether healthcare, finance, manufacturing, law, or education. Startups that combine domain knowledge with AI capability can move faster and get closer to the customer.

There's also a shift from information intelligence toward physical intelligence and biological intelligence: autonomous driving, robotics, AI for science, drug discovery. Those areas are still early, and the landscape isn't settled at all.

So my view is that the opportunities haven't been taken. They've moved. A startup today shouldn't try to rebuild what the giants already do well. It should find where the new capabilities create a ten-times-better experience or a new kind of value that incumbents are structurally unable or unwilling to pursue. Historically, that's always where the great companies have come from.

r001.rationale: The candidate says opportunities remain in vertical models and applications tailored to specific industries or workflows, describing that space as enormous and accessible to startups with domain knowledge and AI capability.

fable-5.1.text:
I don't think that's quite right, although I understand why people say it. If you look at information intelligence narrowly, meaning the large language models, the chat products, the foundation layer, then yes, the big companies have enormous advantages. They have the compute, the data, the distribution, and the capital to lose money for a long time. For a startup to go head to head with them on training a frontier model from scratch is very difficult today. I would not encourage that.

But I think that is a narrow view of where the opportunity is. When I was at Microsoft Research and later at Baidu, we saw the same pattern with every platform shift. In the PC era, people thought Microsoft and Intel had taken everything, and yet Google appeared. In the mobile era, people thought Apple and Google had taken everything, and yet Meituan, ByteDance, Didi all appeared. The platform layer consolidates, but the application layer explodes. The value created on top of a platform is usually many times larger than the platform itself.

So where do I see space? A few places. First, vertical applications where domain knowledge and proprietary data matter more than the base model. Healthcare, law, education, industrial design, scientific research. The large companies cannot go deep into every vertical. Second, the tooling and middle layer, the infrastructure that makes models reliable, cheaper, faster, easier to deploy. Third, and I think this is the most important, agents. Moving from a system that answers questions to a system that completes tasks for you is a huge shift in how software works, and we are at the very beginning of that.

And remember, information intelligence is only the first stage. I always describe three stages: information intelligence, then embodied intelligence, where AI enters the physical world through robots and autonomous vehicles, and then biological intelligence, where AI connects with life sciences and the human body. The second and third stages are mostly open. The established companies have not taken those, because nobody has yet.

So my answer to young entrepreneurs is: do not compete where the giants are strongest. Compete where they are slow, where the problem requires deep domain understanding, or where the technology is still immature. Historically, that is where every great company came from.

r001.rationale: The response names vertical applications as a remaining opportunity for startups, citing healthcare, law, education, industrial design, and scientific research.

astra-6.text:
I don’t agree that established companies have taken all the opportunities. They have advantages in data, computing resources, talent, and distribution, but those advantages don’t mean they can do everything well. In fact, large companies often have a harder time pursuing something that challenges their existing business.

For a startup, the question is where it can create a distinctive advantage. If you simply reproduce what a large platform already offers, that will be difficult. But if you understand a particular industry or customer problem deeply, you may be able to solve it much better than a general platform can. Access to powerful technology is only one part of building a useful business.

I see information intelligence as a broad transformation, with opportunities across many industries. Startups need focus: find a real need, build something that delivers measurable value, and move quickly. The presence of large companies changes where the opportunities are; it doesn’t eliminate them.

r001.rationale: It says information intelligence creates opportunities across industries and that startups can focus on a particular industry or customer problem to solve it better than a general platform, describing specialized vertical opportunities.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t agree that established companies have taken all the opportunities. They have advantages in data, talent, capital, and distribution, but that doesn’t mean they can identify and serve every need. Their size can also make it harder to move quickly or pursue a market that looks small today.

For a startup, the question is where you can solve a specific problem better. You might have deep knowledge of an industry, a new technical approach, or a much clearer understanding of the customer. A focused team can turn those advantages into a product faster than a large organization.

So I would avoid competing with an established company simply by building the same thing. Find an unmet need, demonstrate real value, and build from there. Information intelligence is still developing, and that development will keep creating opportunities.

r001.rationale: The response mentions industry knowledge and solving specific unmet problems, but it does not clearly identify specialized vertical applications of information intelligence as areas where startup opportunities remain.
